summary: Describes Core Based Trees, a design for multicast routing that builds one delivery tree for each group, shared by all senders and receivers. This differs from schemes that build a separate tree per sender. It was published as an experimental protocol and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Multicast needs the network to deliver one message to many receivers. The way routers arrange that delivery decides how much memory they need. This RFC argues for arranging it so the memory depends only on the number of groups, not on the number of senders.

subtitle: An architecture for multicast routing that builds one shared delivery tree per group.

tldr.problem: Multicast algorithms that build a separate delivery tree for every sender make router state grow with the number of senders as well as the number of groups, which does not scale to the thousands of active groups the Internet was expected to carry.
tldr.mechanism: CBT builds one shared tree per group, rooted at a core router that every sender and receiver meets at. The router state then grows as O(G) instead of O(S * G), and data from a sender that is not on the tree is encapsulated with IP-in-IP and unicast to the core.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines an Experimental protocol and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind, and it is now Historic. Its security considerations section says that security considerations are not addressed in the memo.

today: RFC 2201 is a Historic RFC from September 1997. It defines an Experimental protocol and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its security considerations section says that security considerations are not addressed in the memo, and points to RFC 1949 and RFCs 2093 and 2094 for ways of distributing multicast key material.

sections.title: Why Multicast Needed a New Architecture
sections.content:
RFC 2201 describes the architecture of Core Based Trees (CBT), a multicast routing architecture that builds a single delivery tree per group, shared by all of the group's senders and receivers. Most multicast algorithms build one multicast tree per sender subnetwork, the tree being rooted at the sender's subnetwork, and the primary advantage of the shared tree approach is that it typically offers more favourable scaling characteristics than all other multicast algorithms. The protocol itself is described separately in RFC 2189.

The background matters, because the problem is scale. Shared trees were first described by Wall, who concluded that delay will not be minimal, as with shortest-path trees, but can be kept within bounds that may be acceptable. Deering's work in the late 1980s was pioneering: he defined the IP multicast service model and invented algorithms that let hosts join and leave a group arbitrarily. All of Deering's algorithms build source-rooted delivery trees, with one delivery tree per sender subnetwork.

Applications differ widely in what they need. Distributed interactive simulation has strict requirements in terms of join latency, group membership dynamics and group sender populations, far exceeding the requirements of many other multicast applications. The multicast-capable part of the Internet, the MBONE, continued to expand rapidly, and some predictions talked of thousands of groups being present at any one time. The RFC evaluates scalability in terms of network state maintenance, bandwidth efficiency and protocol overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Multicast needs the network to deliver one message to many receivers. The way routers arrange that delivery decides how much memory they need. This RFC argues for arranging it so the memory depends only on the number of groups, not on the number of senders.

sections.title: Source-Based Trees and Their Costs
sections.content:
Source-based tree multicast algorithms are often referred to as dense-mode algorithms: they assume the receiver population densely populates the domain of operation, so the accompanying overhead in state, bandwidth usage and processing costs is justified. That may be the case in a local environment, but wide-area group membership tends to be sparsely distributed throughout the Internet.

The distance-vector multicast algorithm, used by DVMRP, builds a multicast delivery tree using a variant of the Reverse-Path Forwarding technique. When a multicast router receives a data packet, the packet is forwarded over all outgoing interfaces if it arrived on the interface used to reach the source, and discarded otherwise. This is a broadcast-and-prune approach: when a data packet reaches a leaf router that has no membership registered on any of its directly attached subnetworks, that router sends a prune message one hop back towards the source, and the prune propagates upstream for as long as no downstream router has members. The sender and receiver of a prune must cache the source and group pair being reported for a lifetime at the granularity of minutes, and the prune information is removed when that lifetime expires unless it is refreshed, which is why the RFC calls this state soft state. The cost is that routers which do not lead to group members still carry the state overhead of prune messages, and with many thousands of sparsely distributed active groups this technique clearly does not scale.

The link-state multicast algorithm, an instance of which is M-OSPF, has every router flood reachability information and group membership changes throughout the routing domain, so each router has a complete, up-to-date picture of the domain's topology and membership. Each router then computes a shortest-path tree rooted at the sender subnetwork, and multicast data only ever traverses routers leading to members. The flooding of group membership information is the predominant factor preventing this algorithm from being applicable over the wide area, and the processing cost of the Dijkstra calculation to compute the shortest-path tree for each active source is the other limiting factor.
sections.plainLanguage: Two older approaches build a separate tree for each sender. One floods packets everywhere and then prunes back the branches with no listeners, which wastes state on routers that lead nowhere. The other gives every router a full map and makes it compute the best path for each sender, which is slow and floods the network.

sections.title: The Shared-Tree Answer
sections.content:
CBT was designed primarily to address scalability. A shared tree architecture offers an improvement in scalability over source tree architectures by a factor of the number of active sources. Source trees scale O(S * G), since a distinct delivery tree is built per active source. Shared trees eliminate the source factor, because all sources use the same shared tree, and hence a shared tree scales O(G). Applications with many active senders, such as distributed interactive simulation and distributed video gaming, where most receivers are also senders, therefore have a significantly lesser impact on the underlying multicast routing.

The RFC compares the router state needed by CBT and DVMRP for different group sizes with different numbers of active sources. With 10 groups of 20 members each, DVMRP needs 20 router entries when 10 percent of the members send, 100 entries at 50 percent and 200 entries at 100 percent, while CBT needs 10 entries throughout. With 100 groups of 40 members, DVMRP needs 400, 2K and 4K entries at the same three levels, while CBT needs 100 entries. With 1,000 groups of 60 members, DVMRP needs 6K entries at 10 percent of members sending, 30K at 50 percent and 60K at 100 percent, while CBT still needs only 1,000 entries.

Shared trees also incur bandwidth and state savings compared with source trees. The tree only spans a group's receivers, including the links and routers leading to receivers, so there is no cost to routers and links in other parts of the network. Routers between a non-member sender and the delivery tree are not incurred any cost pertaining to multicast, and need not even be multicast-capable, because packets from non-member senders are encapsulated and unicast to a core on the tree.
sections.plainLanguage: One tree per group instead of one per sender. In the RFC's own example, a network with 1,000 groups needs 1,000 entries in CBT but 60,000 in the older approach when every member sends.

sections.title: The Four Design Goals
sections.content:
The CBT shared tree design was geared towards several objectives. Scalability came first: the designers decided not to sacrifice the O(G) scaling character to optimize delay using shortest-path trees, as PIM does, because once multicasting becomes ubiquitous, router state maintenance will be a predominant scaling factor. Delay can still be improved in some circumstances by other means. A broadcast-type lecture with a single sender, or a limited set of infrequently changing senders, could have its core placed in the locality of the sender, allowing the tree to emulate a shortest-path tree while still maintaining its O(G) scaling character.

Robustness is harder to achieve in a shared tree. Source-based tree algorithms are clearly robust: a sender simply sends its data and the intervening routers conspire to get the data where it needs to go, creating state along the way, with no set-up protocol involved. A shared tree's core router maintains the connectivity between all group members and is thus a single point of failure, so protocol mechanisms must ensure that a core failure is detected quickly and the tree reconnected quickly using a replacement core router. Simplicity counts too, because the CBT protocol is relatively simple compared to most other multicast routing protocols, and this simplicity can lead to enhanced performance. Interoperability matters because the Internet is a collection of heterogeneous multicast regions: the protocol interconnecting these regions is currently DVMRP, any region not running DVMRP connects to the DVMRP backbone as a stub region, and CBT has well-defined interoperability mechanisms with DVMRP.
sections.plainLanguage: The design has four goals: use as little router memory as possible, keep working when the core router fails, stay simple, and fit in with the rest of the multicast network.

sections.title: Building and Maintaining the Tree
sections.content:
The protocol is designed to build and maintain a shared multicast distribution tree that spans only those networks and links leading to interested receivers. A host joins by multicasting an IGMP host membership report across its attached link, and the local CBT aware router then starts the tree joining process by generating a JOIN_REQUEST to the next hop on the path towards the group's core router. The join must be explicitly acknowledged with a JOIN_ACK, either by the core router itself or by another router on the path that has already joined successfully. The join sets up transient state in the routers it traverses, consisting of the group, the incoming interface and the outgoing interface, and that state times out unless it is confirmed by a JOIN_ACK from upstream. The JOIN_ACK traverses the reverse path of the join, which is possible because of the transient state. Loops cannot be created in a CBT tree, because there is only one active core per group and the scenarios that might lead to a loop are avoided: if a router's upstream neighbour becomes unreachable, the router immediately flushes all of its downstream branches so they can rejoin individually, and a join message that loops back on itself is never acknowledged and so eventually times out.

The state created by the sending or receiving of a JOIN_ACK is bi-directional, so data can flow either way along a branch, and it is group specific: it holds the group address and a list of local interfaces over which join messages for the group have previously been acknowledged. The upstream interface is called the parent interface and the downstream ones the child interfaces. When a multicast data packet arrives at a router, the router uses the group address as an index into the multicast forwarding cache and forwards a copy over each interface in the entry except the incoming interface. Each router except the core maintains its upstream link by sending periodic keepalive messages, ECHO_REQUEST, to its parent, one message representing all the entries that share that parent, and the parent answers with an ECHO_REPLY that lists the groups for which the link is a child interface.

Control messages that expect a response are retransmitted when no response arrives within the retransmission interval, with an upper bound, typically 3, on the number of retransmissions before an exception condition is raised. For example, the exception procedure for a lack of response to an ECHO_REQUEST is to send a QUIT_NOTIFICATION upstream and a FLUSH_TREE downstream for the group, and to restart the joining process if the router still has group members attached. A non-member sender's data is handled in one of two ways. If the sender's subnet is already attached to the group tree, the local router simply forwards the packet over the outgoing interfaces in that group's forwarding cache entry. If the subnet is not attached, the local designated router encapsulates the packet with IP-in-IP and unicasts it to the group's core router, where it is decapsulated and disseminated over the tree. The routers in between need not know anything about the multicast group and may even be multicast-unaware.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver's router sends a join request towards the core and waits for an answer. The answer comes back the same way and puts the receiver on the tree. From then on, each router copies incoming group traffic out to all its branches except the one it came in on.

sections.title: Core Router Discovery
sections.content:
Core router discovery is by far the most controversial and difficult aspect of shared tree multicast architectures, particularly in the context of inter-domain multicast routing. There have been many proposals over the past three years or so, including advertising core addresses in a multicast session directory, manual placement, and the HPIM approach of strictly dividing the multicast address space into many hierarchical scopes and using explicit advertising of core routers between scope levels.

Two options exist for CBT version 2. The bootstrap mechanism, as currently specified with the PIM sparse mode protocol, applies only to intra-domain core discovery and allows a plug-and-play type of operation with minimal configuration; its disadvantage is that it is much more difficult to affect the shape, and thus the optimality, of the resulting distribution tree, and it must be implemented by all CBT routers within a domain. Manual configuration of leaf routers with core and group mappings is the other option; it imposes a degree of administrative burden, because the mapping for a particular group must be coordinated across all leaf routers to ensure consistency, and it does not scale particularly well. It is likely that better trees result from this method, and it is also the only option currently available for inter-domain core discovery.

In the bootstrap mechanism, a subset of the domain's routers is configured as CBT candidate core routers, and each advertises itself to the domain's Bootstrap Router, which is itself elected dynamically from all or participating routers in the domain. The Bootstrap Router collects those advertisements and periodically advertises a candidate core set to the other routers in the domain using hop-by-hop unicast forwarding. When a router receives an IGMP host membership report from one of its directly attached hosts, it uses a hash function on the reported group address and uses the result as an index into that set, which is how local routers discover which core to use for a group. The hash is tailored so that a small number of consecutive groups always hash to the same core, and a bootstrap message can carry a group mask that limits a candidate core set to a particular range of groups, which helps reduce traffic concentration at the core. If the Bootstrap Router detects a core as unreachable, it deletes it from the set it advertises, and the local router then re-hashes for each affected group and joins the new core after removing the old state.
sections.plainLanguage: Every router has to know which core to join for each group. Either a helper router collects the candidates and tells everyone, and each router picks one by a fixed rule, or an administrator writes the mapping on every leaf router by hand.
